passage: Creche note from Irawati, Monday. Jyoti (14 months) doesn't say words yet, but she listens closely. When I said, "Bring me your shoes," she crawled to the rack and dragged one back. When I asked, "Where's the fan?" she looked up and pointed. At clean-up I said, "Ball in the basket," and she dropped it in and clapped. I'll let her mother know, and keep giving short, one-step requests with a gesture. 😊

qa.q: What did Jyoti bring when asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She dragged one shoe back from the rack.

qa.q: What does Jyoti clapping after dropping the ball in suggest?
qa.a: She seemed pleased with herself for doing what was asked.

qa.q: Why are short requests with a gesture a good plan for Jyoti?
qa.a: They match what she can understand now and give her a clue, so she can succeed while her talking catches up.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She would likely feel reassured that Jyoti understands a lot even without words.

grounding: Shows a baby who cannot yet talk understanding and carrying out simple spoken requests.

passage: Alka is drying chillies on a mat outside their village house. Naveen, fifteen months, toddles close. "No, Naveen, don't touch. Hot," she says, shaking her head. He pulls his hand back and looks up at her face. "Go give this to Dadaji," she says, handing him a steel tumbler. He walks it carefully to his grandfather on the charpai. When Dadaji asks, "Where's the goat?" Naveen turns and points to the shed.

qa.q: Who does Naveen carry the tumbler to?
qa.a: His grandfather, Dadaji, on the charpai.

qa.q: What does Naveen looking at Alka's face after pulling his hand back suggest?
qa.a: He seemed to be checking her face to be sure he had understood, perhaps a little unsure.

qa.q: How could Alka keep building Naveen's understanding?
qa.a: She can keep using simple words with gestures and name things around the farm as they do chores.

qa.q: What would change if Alka assumed Naveen understood nothing because he can't talk yet?
qa.a: She might stop giving him small jobs, and he would miss chances to show what he understands.

grounding: Shows a toddler without speech understanding words and following simple instructions at home.

passage: At the baby song hour in a library in Oslo, Mei, thirteen months, sits on Ingrid's lap. She has no words yet. When the leader sings, "Touch your nose," Mei's finger lands on her cheek, then slides to her nose. At "Clap, clap, clap," she bangs her palms together. As they leave, Ingrid whispers, "Wave bye-bye," and Mei flaps her hand at the leader.

qa.q: Where does Mei's finger land first?
qa.a: On her cheek, before sliding to her nose.

qa.q: What does Mei's finger sliding to her nose suggest she understood?
qa.a: She seemed to understand the word "nose" and corrected her aim to match it.

qa.q: How could Ingrid build on this at home?
qa.a: She could sing the same action songs and use short everyday requests, giving Mei time to respond.

qa.q: How might the song leader see Mei's wave?
qa.a: As a sweet sign that Mei understood "bye-bye" even though she can't say it yet. 🙂

grounding: Shows a baby understanding sung and spoken instructions before she can speak.

passage: I'm Sahil, Himani's cousin. Himani is fourteen months and hardly says any words yet. But today, when her mother said, "Bring your shoes," she toddled to the door and came back with one shoe. When I asked, "Where's the cat?" she turned and pointed under the table. And when her father said, "Wave bye-bye," she waved. She understands much more than she can say.

qa.q: What did Himani bring when her mother asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She came back with one shoe.

qa.q: What does Himani's pointing under the table suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she understood the question and knew where the cat was.

qa.q: How can Himani's family support her understanding of words?
qa.a: They can keep giving simple instructions and naming things around her, and praise her when she responds.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Himani's language?
qa.a: Sahil sees that she understands much more than she can say.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a toddler understanding words and following simple instructions before speaking.

passage:
Monday: Sarita, twelve months, looks up when her aunt Devika says, "Ball!" but doesn't move.

Wednesday: Devika says, "Give me the ball." Sarita holds it out, then pulls it back and laughs.

Saturday: Devika says, "Put the ball in the basket." Sarita crawls over, drops it in, and looks up. Devika claps. Sarita claps too.

qa.q: What did Devika ask Sarita to do on Saturday?
qa.a: She asked her to put the ball in the basket.

qa.q: What does Sarita's laugh on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she understood the request and was playing a teasing game.

qa.q: How did Devika help Sarita learn to follow instructions?
qa.a: She used simple, clear words and gave slightly harder instructions each day.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Sarita puts the ball in the basket?
qa.a: She probably feels delighted, seeing Sarita understand and follow her words.

grounding: Shows a toddler's understanding of spoken words and instructions growing over a week.

passage: "Mehak, bring your shoes. We're going to the park." Manoj, her grandfather, said it once from the doorway. Mehak, fifteen months, who could only say "Nana" and "no", looked at him, looked at the shoe rack, toddled over and came back with one sandal and one of his slippers. He laughed and held up his own foot. "Yours, beta, not mine." She went back, dropped the slipper and returned with her second sandal.

qa.q: What did Mehak bring back the first time?
qa.a: One sandal and one of his slippers.

qa.q: Why did Mehak go back to the shoe rack a second time?
qa.a: She understood what her grandfather meant and wanted to get it right, and seemed pleased to help.

qa.q: How could Manoj keep building Mehak's understanding of words?
qa.a: Keep giving short, clear requests during daily routines and show her with gestures when she gets part of it wrong.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj to see her follow instructions she can't say yet?
qa.a: He finds it funny and delightful, and it shows him she understands far more than her two words.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a spoken instruction while she can say only two words.

passage:
"Sunaina, bath time. Can you put the duck in the bucket?" Deepak asked.
Sunaina, not yet talking, picked up the yellow duck and dropped it in with a splash.
"Now give Papa the towel."
She looked around, then pointed at the towel on the chair.
"Yes, that one. Can you bring it?"
She dragged it over, half on the floor.
"And where's the soap?"
She clapped her hands over her ears and ran to the bedroom, giggling.
"Ah. You understood that one too," Deepak said.

qa.q: What did Sunaina drop in the bucket?
qa.a: The yellow duck.

qa.q: What does Sunaina running away giggling at the word "soap" suggest?
qa.a: She clearly understood the word and felt playful and a bit mischievous, since she didn't want the bath yet.

qa.q: How could Deepak turn bath time into more listening practice?
qa.a: Keep giving one simple step at a time, like putting the duck in, and praise each step she follows.

qa.q: How does Deepak see Sunaina's giggling escape?
qa.a: He takes it with humour, as proof she understands "soap" even though she can't say it.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cannot yet talk understanding and acting on several spoken requests.

passage:
Playgroup note from Parveen, the week before Eid
Farida (20 months) still says only a few words, but she follows much more. Today I said, "Put the mehndi cones back in the box," and she did, one by one. When I said, "Wash hands, then snack," she walked to the tap first. She looked confused when I asked her to fetch "the blue one," so I pointed and she got it. I'll keep adding gestures to new words and share this with her family 🙂

qa.q: What did Farida put back in the box?
qa.a: The mehndi cones.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Parveen asked for "the blue one"?
qa.a: She seemed confused, perhaps unsure which item was meant, until Parveen pointed.

qa.q: Which choice by Parveen helped most, and why?
qa.a: Pointing when Farida got stuck, because it linked the new words to something she could see.

qa.q: How might Farida's family feel reading this note?
qa.a: Reassured that she understands a lot even though she talks little, and glad to know how to help.

grounding: Shows a toddler following two-step spoken instructions before she can say much herself.

passage: On Baisakhi morning in their village near Moga, Bebe Baljeet was tying her hair when she said, "Pradeep, bring me my chunni. The yellow one, on the charpai." Pradeep, sixteen months, had no words yet except "ma" and "ba". He looked at the charpai, toddled over, and tugged the yellow cloth until it slid off. He dragged it across the yard to her. "Shabaash!" Bebe laughed. Pradeep beamed and went back for her shoes, which nobody had asked for.

qa.q: What colour was Bebe's chunni?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's beaming show?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud and happy at being praised for bringing the chunni.

qa.q: What could Bebe do to keep building Pradeep's understanding?
qa.a: Give short, clear requests with one or two details, point if needed, and praise him when he follows them.

qa.q: How might Bebe see Pradeep bringing her shoes too?
qa.a: Bebe probably found it funny and sweet, a sign he understands and wants to help.

grounding: On Baisakhi morning, a toddler without words follows his grandmother's two-part instruction.

passage: In Nairobi the long rains had kept everyone indoors for days. When the sun finally broke through one April afternoon, Wanjiru, Aiko's nanny, said, "Aiko, get your boots. We're going outside." Aiko, fourteen months, couldn't say "boots" yet. But she crawled straight to the door, patted her red rain boots, and looked up. "Yes, those!" Wanjiru said. Aiko squealed and held up one foot.

qa.q: What colour were Aiko's rain boots?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: How was Aiko feeling when she squealed and held up her foot?
qa.a: Aiko felt excited and happy about going outside after days indoors.

qa.q: How can Wanjiru keep helping Aiko understand words?
qa.a: Keep naming things clearly and confirming, like 'Yes, those!', whenever Aiko shows she understood.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel when Aiko pats the boots?
qa.a: Wanjiru would likely feel pleased and delighted to see Aiko understand the word before she can say it.

grounding: After the long rains in Kenya, a toddler shows she understands 'boots' before she can say it.

passage: I'm Eshaan, Ujjwal's cousin. The week before Diwali, Chachi gave Ujjwal a cleaning job too. He's only eighteen months and says maybe three words. "Ujjwal, put the ball in the box," she said. He picked up the ball, walked to the box and dropped it in. "Now the car." The car went in. "Now give Eshaan Bhaiya a hug." He came and hugged my leg. I'm not sure he knew every word, but he got all three right.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal put in the box first?
qa.a: The ball.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have felt hugging Eshaan's leg?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed happy and affectionate, pleased to be part of the game.

qa.q: Why did Chachi's instructions work well for Ujjwal?
qa.a: They were short, one step at a time, and about familiar objects, so he could follow without speaking.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Ujjwal's understanding?
qa.a: Eshaan is impressed that Ujjwal followed all three, though unsure he knew every word.

grounding: An older cousin watches a nearly wordless toddler follow simple instructions during Diwali cleaning.

passage:
December, first cold morning: Urmila Nani says, "Zeenat, bring your socks." Zeenat, fourteen months, just smiles.

Next week: Nani says it again, pointing at the socks. Zeenat crawls over and pats them.

Makar Sankranti morning: Nani, busy with the til laddoos, says, "Zeenat, socks," without pointing. Zeenat toddles to the basket, pulls out one sock, and brings it to her.

qa.q: What was Nani making on Makar Sankranti morning?
qa.a: She was busy with the til laddoos.

qa.q: How might Urmila Nani have felt when Zeenat brought the sock?
qa.a: Nani was likely delighted and proud, since Zeenat understood without any pointing.

qa.q: How did Nani help Zeenat's understanding grow over the weeks?
qa.a: She repeated the same simple words in daily routines and pointed at first, then let Zeenat try without help.

qa.q: What might Zeenat feel when she brings the sock to Nani?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel pleased and proud to be helping.

grounding: Across winter weeks, a toddler who does not yet speak comes to understand and follow a simple instruction.

passage:
On the fifth night of Navratri, the building compound in Ahmedabad was lit with lamps. Lavanya, who was not yet talking, sat on her mother's lap in her tiny chaniya choli.

"Lavanya, give this flower to Paati," Vidya said, pointing at the old woman beside them.

Lavanya looked at the marigold, looked at Paati, then wriggled down and pushed the flower into Paati's hand.

Paati kissed her fingers.

qa.q: What did Lavanya give to Paati?
qa.a: She gave Paati a marigold.

qa.q: How might Paati have felt when Lavanya handed her the flower?
qa.a: Paati was likely touched and happy, which is why she kissed Lavanya's fingers.

qa.q: How can Vidya keep supporting Lavanya's understanding of words?
qa.a: Keep giving short, clear instructions with names and objects Lavanya knows, and praise her when she follows them.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel watching Lavanya follow her words?
qa.a: Vidya would likely feel proud and happy that Lavanya understood even before speaking.

grounding: During Navratri, a toddler who is not yet speaking understands and follows a simple spoken request.

passage:
"Jomon, where's the star?" Harish asked, sitting by the paper lantern on the balcony. It was Christmas week in Kochi.

Jomon, fifteen months, looked straight up and pointed at the lantern.

"And where's Appa's nose?"

Jomon reached out and grabbed it.

Harish's wife laughed from the kitchen. "He can't say ten words, but he understands everything."

"Jomon, bring the ball."

Jomon crawled off and came back with a slipper.

"Close enough," said Harish.

qa.q: Where did Jomon point when asked about the star?
qa.a: He looked straight up and pointed at the lantern.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Jomon brought a slipper?
qa.a: Harish seemed amused and warm, laughing it off with "Close enough".

qa.q: How can Harish keep supporting Jomon's understanding?
qa.a: Keep asking simple, playful questions about familiar things and show the right object gently when Jomon gets it wrong.

qa.q: How does Harish's wife see Jomon's language?
qa.a: She sees that Jomon understands much more than he can say.

grounding: At Christmas, a toddler who says few words shows he understands simple questions and instructions.

passage:
Playgroup note, Wednesday
Himani still says only "ba" and "ma", but she understands far more. When I said, "Bring me your shoes," she toddled to the rack, brought one shoe, then went back for the second. At clean-up I asked her to put the duck in the basket, and she did. At pickup her brother Ojas asked, "Himani, where's your bag?" She pointed straight at the hook. Ojas stared. "She knows!" I'll keep giving her short, clear requests. 😊
Teacher Shobha

qa.q: What did Himani do when Teacher Shobha asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She toddled to the rack, brought one shoe, then went back for the second.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when she pointed at the hook for Ojas?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and pleased to show she understood, even though she can't say the words yet.

qa.q: How could Himani's family build on what she understands?
qa.a: They could give her short, clear requests and name objects as she touches them, then wait for her to show she understood.

qa.q: Why was Ojas surprised at pickup?
qa.a: Ojas probably thought his little sister couldn't understand much because she barely talks, so her quick pointing surprised him.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cannot yet speak much understanding words and following simple instructions.
